title: Why we're building an Agentic LMS
summary: What an Agentic LMS is, why K-12 schools now have to show how much students learned, and what Flint's Agentic LMS does today.
body_markdown:
Flint is building an Agentic LMS because, on the LMS, education is now moving faster than the technology. I didn't expect to write that sentence. K-12 schools and districts are now expected to show how much their students learned, and the LMS most of them use was built to record what was assigned, what was turned in and what grade it got. An Agentic LMS is a learning management system that knows the course and each student, carries what happened last week into today, and takes the next step without waiting to be asked. This post covers what changed for schools, what an Agentic LMS is, what Flint does today and what we're still building.


## Education is moving faster than the LMS


Most edtech is sold on the idea that software leads and schools catch up. With the LMS, I see the opposite. Most weeks I'm on calls with principals, IT directors and curriculum leaders, and their goals have moved further than the system their teachers log into every day.


An LMS answers three questions about every piece of work: was it assigned, was it turned in, and what grade did it get. Schools still need those answers. They need a gradebook, due dates and one place for assignments. But those answers are now the floor, and school leaders are being asked for much more.


## Schools now have to show how much students learned


The priorities of schools and districts have shifted a lot in the last five years. What schools used to measure is now the minimum. Leaders are expected to show how much learning happened, and a score on its own doesn't show that. A few signs of the shift:


- States measure growth as well as proficiency. Student growth percentiles, which compare a student's progress with students who started at a similar score, are the most common growth measure in state accountability systems, used by 24 states and Washington, D.C., according to the Education Commission of the States'[2024 50-state comparison](https://www.ecs.org/50-state-comparison-school-accountability-systems-2024/) .
- At least 36 states count chronic absenteeism in school accountability, per the same comparison, so attendance and engagement sit next to test scores.
- At least 21 states have written a portrait of a graduate, a list of the skills students should leave school with,[EdWeek Market Brief reported](https://marketbrief.edweek.org/meeting-district-needs/what-is-a-portrait-of-a-graduate-and-how-can-k-12-companies-use-them-to-understand-districts/2025/11) in November 2025. In California, 104 districts have one, including all of the state's largest.


A grade at the end of a unit can't answer the questions behind those changes. Growth has to be seen over time. A portrait of a graduate asks about skills like problem solving and communication, which a final grade doesn't record. Catching a student who is slipping means noticing before the failing grade exists.


## A traditional LMS can't see learning


In most schools, the LMS runs from the top down. Admins set it up, teachers push materials through it, and students download the reading, upload the essay and take the quiz. The learning happens somewhere else: notes in Google Docs, flashcards in Quizlet, a question to ChatGPT at 11pm. The LMS knows an essay was submitted at 11:58pm. It has no record of what the student understood, where they got stuck or how they got unstuck.


Schools have filled the gap by adding tools on top of the LMS: one for tutoring, one for quizzes, one for writing feedback, one for analytics. Each tool sees a slice of a student's work, and the slices rarely connect. As I wrote in my[letter to Flint schools](https://flintk12.com/agentic-lms-letter-from-sohan) , "the LMS as it stands today is an antiquated piece of software that is holding schools back, and adding more edtech tools on top won't change that reality."


Flint's answer is to be the place where the learning happens, for admins, teachers and students. The work happens in Flint, so Flint can see the learning and act on it.


## School leaders are already asking for it


Schools brought this idea to us. School leaders have been reaching out to tell us they aren't satisfied with their LMS and want to use Flint in its place. When one of our account executives described where Flint is going, a curriculum director answered, "We would love to be involved, because that product is desperately needed in the world."


The calls since then have moved past whether to the practical details. School leaders ask how a teacher's years of materials would move over from their current LMS, how competencies would be graded next to subject grades, and how a pre-K student who can't type yet would turn in work. Those are the questions people ask when they plan to switch, and they are shaping what we build first.


## What is an Agentic LMS?


An Agentic LMS is a learning management system that takes steps toward a goal without being prompted each time. It comes down to three things:


- The LMS knows the context: the course, the standards, the assignment, the class's history and each student's history.
- It works across time, carrying what happened last week into what it does today.
- It makes the first move. When it notices something, it does something about it instead of waiting to be opened.


All three depend on the learning happening inside the system. A tool bolted onto an LMS has no course context, no memory of the learning and no standing to act.


These examples show where we're heading for each person in a school. The next section covers what Flint does today.


- A student is partway through an assignment. The tutor sees from the pattern of the student's attempts that the real gap is a skill from a unit three weeks ago, and works on that skill first. Later that week, with a unit test on the calendar, it offers practice on the same skill without being asked.
- Before class, a teacher opens Flint, which has already read last night's work. It tells the teacher that eleven students missed the same step in one problem, names the misconception, and suggests a warm-up that targets it.
- An admin oversees a student whose attendance dips, whose work in Flint drops off and whose grades slip in two courses. Flint flags the pattern before the quarter closes, records it against the school's tiered supports, and later shows whether the support helped.


## What Flint does today


Flint already covers many LMS basics, and it records parts of the learning that a traditional LMS can't see:


- Every class has a gradebook, a calendar of what's due, and a Curriculum tab where teachers bring in their own standards or adopt ready-made standards for all 40 AP courses.
- Sparky, Flint's AI, tutors students toward those standards in each activity, and teachers can read their students' conversations with Sparky.
- After students submit their work, teachers see how each student did on each standard, in addition to the overall grade.
- The Outcomes tab shows teachers and school leaders how students who use Flint the least and the most perform on a learning measure they choose, across a class or a school.
- [Paste history](https://help.flintk12.com/articles/seeing-your-students-paste-history) shows teachers what students pasted into their messages to Sparky, so they can tell when an answer came from somewhere else.
- When a teacher asks Sparky to draft an activity, nothing reaches students until the teacher reviews the draft and creates the activity.
- Flint imports class rosters from systems like Canvas, Google Classroom, Veracross and Blackbaud.


The monthly[What's New](https://flintk12.com/whats-new/july-2026) posts show each of these as it shipped. The part Flint doesn't do yet is the part in the examples above: spotting patterns across weeks of a student's work and starting the next step on its own. That's what we're building over the coming months.

## FAQ


### Why is Flint building an Agentic LMS?


Schools are now expected to show how much students learned, and a traditional LMS records only what was assigned, submitted and graded. When students do their work in Flint, Flint can see the learning and act on it.


### Do we have to replace our current LMS to use Flint?


No. You can use Flint as your LMS, or keep your current LMS and use Flint alongside it. Flint imports rosters from systems like Canvas, Google Classroom, Veracross and Blackbaud.


### Does Flint's AI act without the teacher?


When Sparky drafts an activity, nothing reaches students until the teacher reviews the draft and creates the activity. Teachers can read their students' conversations with Sparky. If a teacher turns on auto-grading for a chat activity, students see Sparky's grade before the teacher reviews it.


### When can my school try Flint's Agentic LMS?


Flint is running pilots with schools that want to help design the Agentic LMS, and many of them start next semester. Teachers can start using Flint for free today, and schools can book a demo to talk about a pilot.
